Well, your intuition is off. Given a random sample of numbers 0-999, the probability of collisions isn't great. Think about it like this: once we have a number, the probability of a collision is only 1/1000 while the probability of a new number is 999/1000. By three numbers, we have a probability of 999*998/1000000 = about 99.7% of having no collisions. The probability of no collisions remains rather high for quite a while until we get to a fairly large sample. Eventually it becomes 0 when we reach a sample of 1000 numbers due to the pigeonhole principle (guaranteed collision by the 1001st number). Your failure of intuition comes by not understanding that you are unlikely to have any collisions until pretty late in this experiment. That's why most of the values are distinct and only about 9.2% are collisions, on average. Most of those 9.2% come after lots and lots of distinct values are encountered.

Furthermore, you are misunderstanding the difference between probability and expectation. On average, we expect all the numbers to appear by 11 days. However, that doesn't mean it's a guarantee. If we ran this experiment over and over, we would come up with this average value. Of course it is always possible for some numbers to be excluded in eleven days, but the probability is a bit smaller than your intuition would suggest. The probability that a number is excluded in eleven days is slightly larger than the probability that a number appears twice in eleven days, with an average of approximately once per eleven days.
